t.srinagar@34.1,74.8:
This is the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, a city of canals, wooden houseboats and old mosques, where the Mughal emperors laid out gardens such as Shalimar and Nishat to take advantage of the cool air and the view across the lake. Willow, chinar and poplar trees line the roads, and in autumn the chinar leaves turn a deep orange.

The Srinagar–Leh highway starts here and climbs towards Ladakh, one of the great high roads of the world. The first stage is gentle, running east along the Sindh river valley through Kangan to Sonamarg, a meadow surrounded by snow peaks, and then the road climbs steeply to the Zoji La, a pass at about 3,500 metres, which is the gateway to Ladakh. The surface varies from good to broken, and sections can be muddy, narrow and exposed, with drops and heavy truck traffic. Traffic is controlled in one direction at a time over the pass, so timing matters. The pass usually opens in spring and closes with the first big snows, so check the conditions before you set off.

Kashmir has a long cultural history, with a mix of Hindu, Buddhist and Islamic traditions, and its crafts, including carpets, papier-mâché and shawls, are known throughout India. The food is rich, with wazwan banquets of lamb and kahwa, a green tea flavoured with saffron and almonds. The region has seen conflict, and security checkpoints are common, so carry your documents and check the latest news and travel advice before you ride.

Fuel is no problem in Srinagar, which has stations throughout, and it is essential to fill up here before leaving, as stations become sparse beyond Sonamarg. Kargil, the next town of any size, is about two hundred kilometres away, and the distance and altitude make it a long day.

Spend an hour on the lake if you have time. A shikara ride at dawn, with mist on the water and the mountains in the distance, sets the tone for the road ahead.
t.giri complex of monuments@33.7,72.9:
The valley around Taxila is one of those places where the past is stacked in layers, and you can feel it as soon as you leave the road. Just north-west of Islamabad and Rawalpindi, in the foothills of the Margalla Hills, the broad plain was for more than a thousand years a crossroads for traders, armies, monks and scholars moving between Central Asia, India and the Persian world. UNESCO listed the ruins in 1980, and the Giri complex belongs to this wider landscape.

The great age of the region was Gandhara, a Buddhist kingdom that mixed Indian, Persian and Greek influences. According to tradition, Alexander the Great marched through in 326 BC and was received by the local ruler, and later the Mauryan emperor Ashoka held the city, and the Kushans made it a centre of Buddhist learning and art. Monasteries, stupas and universities spread across the surrounding hills, and the ruins of several of them can be visited in the valley. Gandharan sculpture, in which the Buddha looks something like a Greek god with wavy hair and a robe, is one of the great hybrids of art history.

It is the sort of place where the real pleasure is in the setting, the dry hills, the terraced fields and the haze over the plain, and in having it largely to yourself on a weekday.

The riding in the area is easy. The roads from Islamabad are good, though traffic around the cities is heavy, and the lanes close to the sites are narrow and dusty. Watch for livestock, carts and motorbikes carrying whole families. Summer heat is severe, with temperatures well over forty degrees, so go in the cooler months of October to March or early in the morning. Haze from dust and smoke can reduce the view.

Fuel is easy, since Islamabad is about fifteen kilometres away, and the highway towns have stations. Small tea stalls near the sites sell chai and samosas. Taxila Museum, in town, is a short drive and shows many of the finds from the valley.

Go with a flask of water, a hat and some patience, and give yourself time to wander.
t.giri mosque and tombs@33.7,72.9:
Not everything in the Taxila valley is Buddhist, and the Giri mosque and tombs are a reminder of a later chapter. The Islamic centuries left their mark here too, in small mosques, tombs and shrines on the plain, built after the Muslim dynasties arrived from the north-west and the old monasteries had fallen into ruin. UNESCO's Taxila listing, from 1980, covers a long run of history, and the Islamic period is part of it.

The details of this particular mosque and its tombs, who built them and when, are not facts I can state with confidence, and the best guide is the local sign or the site custodian. What you can say is that the setting is typical of the valley, with a modest building of brick and plaster in a dry, open landscape, and that these small monuments were part of everyday religious life long after the grand Buddhist foundations had faded.

The district itself is full of interest. The Grand Trunk Road, one of the oldest roads in South Asia, runs close by, following a route used since the Mauryan period and rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri in the sixteenth century. Mughal emperors passed along it on their way between Kabul and Lahore, and the Sikh armies of Ranjit Singh later swept through. The valley's villages grow wheat, maize and sugar cane, and the smell of woodsmoke and baking bread drifts across the fields at dusk.

For motorcyclists, the area is a relaxed afternoon out of Islamabad. The roads are generally well surfaced but busy, with trucks, buses and overloaded rickshaws, and the highway has hazards such as sudden stops and drivers who overtake on blind bends. Smaller roads are quieter but dusty. Summer heat is severe, and the best season is autumn to spring. Haze can limit visibility, and fog sometimes comes down in winter mornings.

Fuel is no problem near the capital, with stations at regular intervals, and Rawalpindi, a little over twenty kilometres away, has a lively bazaar and plenty of repair shops. Small cafes sell tea, kebabs and fresh bread at low prices.

Plan to arrive before the afternoon heat, and take a hat, water and a small donation for the custodian, who is usually happy to talk.
t.khanpur cave@33.8,72.9:
Khanpur Cave sits in the hills north-west of Islamabad, close to the Khanpur Dam and the green reservoir that spreads below the town of Khanpur, and it is one of the older places on this ride. Archaeological work in the cave has found evidence of prehistoric occupation, with people sheltering here long before any of the cities and monasteries in the valley were built. It is a reminder that the Taxila region was inhabited for a very long time before it became famous.

The cave is modest, a rock shelter in a dry, scrubby hill, and what makes it affecting is the idea of people living here in the Stone Age, hunting in the forests of the foothills and drinking from the Haro River. The river runs down from the Margalla Hills and the hills of Hazara, and the dam built across it in the 1980s now supplies water to Islamabad and Rawalpindi, as well as irrigating fields. On the lake, there are boats and picnic spots, and families come on weekends.

The surrounding scenery is green by the standards of the region. Low hills covered in thorny scrub and olive-like trees give way to terraced fields, and in spring the almond and peach blossom brightens the hillsides. The air in the foothills is clear in winter and hazy in summer. Monkeys sit along the roadsides, and birds of prey wheel over the lake. The area is part of the wider Taxila region, and the dam, the cave and the ancient sites make a good day out together.

For a rider the roads here are narrow and winding, with sharper bends than on the plain and sudden climbs, and the tarmac is usually decent but patched. Dust, loose gravel and slow trucks are common, and in the monsoon, from about July to September, landslides and washouts can block roads. Weekends bring heavy traffic to the lake. Ride carefully on the bends, and keep an eye out for livestock.

Fuel is sold in Khanpur and on the main road, though Islamabad, about fifteen kilometres away, offers a much wider choice, and Haripur to the north has bigger markets. Bring water and snacks, as the cave itself has no facilities.

Visit on a clear morning in winter or early spring, when the hills are green and the air is cool. A flask of tea on the shore makes a nice end.
t.rohtas fort@33.0,73.6:
Rohtas is a fort built with a grudge. Sher Shah Suri, the Afghan ruler who drove the Mughal emperor Humayun out of India in the 1540s, ordered it to be raised in the Salt Range foothills, partly to command the road to Kabul and partly to keep the Gakhar tribe of the region in check. The Gakhars refused to cooperate with him, and the fort became a standing rebuke. Work began in 1541 and continued for years, though it was never fully completed, and Sher Shah died in 1545, before he could see his dream finished.

The scale is astonishing. A wall of roughly four kilometres, up to ten or so metres thick in places, winds along the ridge, with twelve main gates and dozens of bastions, in rough, honey-coloured sandstone. The Sohail Gate, with its carved stonework and Quranic inscriptions, is the most handsome, and the Langar Khani Gate and Khwas Khani Gate are also impressive. The fort was designed more to be a mighty statement than a practical garrison, and it was apparently never taken by force. The Mughals under Humayun returned to power in 1555, and the fort's role faded. UNESCO listed it in 1997.

The surroundings are dry, rocky and quiet, a landscape of ravines, scrub and low hills with the Kahan river valley below. There is not much shade, so the walk around the walls is hot work, and the views over the plain are wide. Wild flowers appear after spring rain. A small village sits at the foot of the fort, with a tea stall, and the people are curious and friendly.

The riding is straightforward, with the Grand Trunk Road and the roads from Jhelum, about fourteen kilometres away, in decent condition, though crowded with trucks and buses. The last stretch is narrow and sometimes rough, and summers are severely hot, so go in winter or spring. In the monsoon the ravines can flood.

Jhelum has fuel, banks and plenty of places to eat, and you should fill up there. Take water, a hat and sun protection, since the fort offers little shade.

Allow at least two hours to see the main gates and walls, and aim for the late afternoon, when the light on the stone turns warm and the heat eases.
t.abbottabad@34.1,73.2:
Abbottabad sits in a cool green bowl of pine-covered hills at about 1,250 metres, and for a rider coming up from the plains the first thing you notice is the air. After the heat of Islamabad and the Punjab plains, it feels like stepping into a different country. The town was founded in the 1850s by James Abbott, a British officer who was struck by the climate and the beauty of the area, and it kept its colonial bones: a cantonment of broad avenues, old schools, and a military academy at nearby Kakul. Today it is a city of around a hundred thousand people in the Hazara region, with a bustling bazaar and a university.

Abbottabad gained a very different sort of fame in 2011, when the world's most wanted man was found in a compound on the edge of town. That story is not what most visitors come for, and locals can be weary of it. What they will tell you about instead is the climate, the schools and the surrounding hills, where summer visitors flock to Nathia Gali and Ayubia, a national park of forests and walking paths on the slopes above. The Thandiani ridge, on the north side, has views over to the Kashmir mountains on a clear day.

For the Karakoram Highway, Abbottabad is the real beginning. The road from Islamabad joins the old Silk Road route here, and climbs through the foothills toward Havelian, where the highway proper starts. From here you head north into increasingly dramatic country, with the Indus gorge to come. The road surface is generally good on this section, with gentle curves and heavy traffic of trucks, buses and rickshaws, so overtaking requires patience and good judgement.

Fuel and services are plentiful: there are petrol stations, mechanics, ATMs and decent restaurants, and the bazaar sells everything from dried fruit to spare parts. This is the place to fill up, eat and stock up on water before the mountain stages, because services get thinner farther north. The Hindko-speaking locals are friendly, and a rider on a foreign bike will draw a curious crowd.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Summers bring monsoon rain and landslides on the hill roads, while winter nights can be cold, and snow occasionally dusts the heights around town.
t.besham@34.9,72.9:
Besham is a bazaar town clinging to the bank of the Indus, and it earns its place on the Karakoram Highway the way many towns on that road do: it is where everyone stops. The highway comes up from the lowlands through a deep gorge, the Indus running brown and fast beside it, and by the time you reach Besham the mountains are close and steep on both sides. The altitude is modest, but the sense of enclosure is complete. Locals will tell you that Besham is where the Himalayas really begin, and a rider arriving at midday with sore knees will agree.

The town sits at the junction for the road up to Swat, over the Shangla Pass, one of the old routes into the northern valleys. That makes it a crossroads for buses, trucks and Land Cruisers, and the bazaar is lively, with dhabas serving chicken karahi, daal and fresh naan, and tea stalls on every corner. A hot meal here is a good one. The population is mainly Pashtun and Kohistani, and the area has been a trade route for centuries, long before the Chinese helped build the highway in the 1960s and 70s, at the cost of many lives.

The road in and out is the real attraction. The Karakoram Highway between Besham and Thakot is cut into the rock face above the river, with sharp bends, narrow stretches and sheer drops. Landslides are common, especially in the monsoon, and the surface can be broken in places, so slow down, and ride in daylight. The reward is views of the Indus gorge that few roads in the world can match, with the river frothing over boulders far below and terraced fields climbing the slopes.

Fuel is available in Besham, as are basic hotels, mechanics and shops. Battagram, to the north-east, is larger. Fill up here, because the road beyond gets longer between pumps and the quality of fuel varies. The 2005 earthquake devastated this region, and the rebuilt towns show the scars, but local hospitality is warm.

Late spring and autumn are the best times to ride. Summer rain brings rockfalls and delays, and winter can close higher sections of the road. Check conditions locally, as the situation changes quickly.
t.islamabad@33.7,73.0:
Islamabad is the start of one of the great roads of the world, the Karakoram Highway, which climbs from the plains of the Punjab through Hazara and the Indus gorge to the Khunjerab Pass on the Chinese border. The capital itself is a young city, planned in the 1960s by the Greek architect Constantinos Doxiadis to replace Karachi, laid out on a grid of numbered sectors with wide avenues and trees, and tucked below the green wall of the Margalla Hills. Rawalpindi, the older garrison town next door, is far more crowded and loud, and the two together form one urban area.

The city has some places worth a stop before you leave. The Faisal Mosque, with its tent-like shape and four minarets, stands at the foot of the hills and is one of the largest mosques in the world, and a short climb up to Daman-e-Koh gives a view over the sectors to the plains. The hills hold leopards and monkeys, and the evening smell of woodsmoke and cooking drifts down from the villages. The Pakistan Monument, a petal-shaped structure on a hill, is a landmark.

Riding out is a lesson in patience at first. The traffic through Rawalpindi and the Grand Trunk Road is dense, with rickshaws, buses and trucks painted in elaborate colours, and you need to be alert and ride defensively. After Hasan Abdal, the highway begins to climb through Haripur toward Abbottabad and Mansehra, with greener hills, terraces and the first views of snow in the distance. Then the road descends to the Indus at Besham, and from there it is a dramatic gorge with cliffs and the river roaring below. Landslides and rockfalls can close sections, particularly after the monsoon rains of July and August, so check conditions before you go.

Fuel is plentiful in the capital and along the highway, but take care to fill up before the long mountain stretches and carry cash, as cards are not accepted in many places. Travellers should also check current advice and any permit or security requirements for the north, which can change. A cup of sweet milky tea at a roadside dhaba is the standard break, and the food, from grilled chicken to hot naan, is excellent.
t.islamabad@33.7,73.1:
Seen as a base for day rides rather than a destination, Islamabad has two historic targets within reach, and they pull in opposite directions. West, about thirty-five kilometres away, lies Taxila, the ruins of a centre of Gandhara culture where Buddhism and Greek-influenced art met around two thousand years ago. The stupas at Dharmarajika and the monastery at Jaulian stand among dry hills, and the museum holds remarkable sculptures of the Buddha with a face that looks almost Mediterranean. South-east, along the Grand Trunk Road past Jhelum, stands Rohtas Fort, a vast sixteenth-century fortress built by the Afghan ruler Sher Shah Suri to guard against the Mughals, whose huge walls and gates follow the ridge above a river.

Both rides use the same corridor. The motorway, the M1 toward Peshawar and the M2 toward Lahore, is fast and well kept, and a good way to get clear of the city quickly. After that the older Grand Trunk Road offers more flavour, with roadside stalls, trucks and rural life, but also more risk, because vehicles stop and turn without warning and the surface can be broken. Hot summer days between May and September can be brutal, so start early and carry water, and the monsoon in July and August brings heavy downpours and sudden flooding of the low roads.

The landscape is a surprise to many visitors. Beyond the capital the Potohar plateau is a land of eroded ravines, scrubby hills and wheat fields, with salt-range ridges rising to the south. Winter days from November to February are dry and bright, with a clear air and a light haze at sunset, and these are the best months for riding and for walking around ruins.

Islamabad has fuel on every main road, and the sector markets have plenty of places to eat and repair a bike. Along the Grand Trunk Road, stations are frequent, but try to keep a reserve. Always carry some cash and your documents, as police checkpoints are common, and keep a little patience with them. The restaurants on the lower slopes of the Margalla Hills are a good place for a late dinner after a long day of ruins and dust.
t.naran@34.9,73.7:
Naran is a mountain town in the Kaghan valley of northern Pakistan, at about 2,400 metres, and it is the last substantial settlement before the road climbs to the Babusar Pass. The valley is long, green and steep, with the Kunhar river rushing through it and pine forest on the slopes, and snow peaks closing the horizon. The town itself is a long strip of hotels, bazaars and restaurants along the river, busy in summer with Pakistani families escaping the heat of the plains. Lake Saif ul Malook, a turquoise lake beneath Malika Parbat, the Queen of the Mountains, lies about ten kilometres away and can be reached by a rough jeep track.

Legend says that a prince, Saif ul Malook, fell in love with a fairy, and the lake is the place where they met, a story told in many versions across the Kaghan valley. The mountains above Naran are part of the western Himalaya, and Malika Parbat, at about 5,290 metres, is the highest in the area. The people of the valley are Gujjars and Kohistanis, who keep cattle and goats, and in summer, they move to high pastures.

The Babusar Pass road, which leaves Naran, climbs to about 4,170 metres, then descends to Chilas in the Indus valley. It is a spectacular, high-altitude road, with steep hairpins, rough surface, and sections of gravel and washout, and it is open only in summer, from about June to October, depending on snow. Landslides are common, and the road can be closed for days. Weather changes fast, with cold wind, rain or snow, even in July. Altitude can be a problem, so ride slowly.

Naran has fuel stations and workshops, but supplies can run short in the busy season, so top up when you can. Food is simple and hearty: trout from the river, dal, rice and naan, with sweet tea. Hotels range from basic to comfortable, and in July and August, they fill up. Check the road conditions with local police before the pass, and set off early to avoid afternoon storms. The air in the morning is cold and clear, and the mountains glow in the sunrise.
t.astana@51.2,71.4:
Astana is a capital city that was assembled in the middle of the steppe by decision. It was Akmola, then Tselinograd in the Soviet era, then Akmola again, and became Kazakhstan's capital in 1997, when the government moved from Almaty. Since then, it has been transformed by a huge construction programme, with futuristic towers and bold architecture rising above the flat plain. The name changed to Nur-Sultan in 2019 and back to Astana in 2022, a bit of political confusion that you may see reflected on older signs and maps.

The skyline is a mix of showpieces. The Baiterek tower, a golden orb on a white stem, symbolises a mythical tree of life; the Khan Shatyr, a giant transparent tent designed by Norman Foster, houses shops and even an indoor beach; and the Palace of Peace and Reconciliation is a glass pyramid. The Ishim river curves through town, with promenades along its banks. It is a city best seen at dusk, when the lights come on and the boulevards fill with families. It is also one of the coldest capitals in the world, with winter temperatures that can reach thirty below.

The riding is flat, wide and fast. Roads leaving the city head across an endless, windy steppe, and in summer the heat is dry and the grass turns gold. Highways are generally decent, with long straight sections and speed cameras, and driving styles can be bold. Spring and autumn are short; summer is the best time for a motorcycle, and winter is out of the question for most riders. The wind across the plain is constant, so expect to lean into it.

As a stop, Astana is as well served as any capital. Fuel, dealerships, repair shops, banks, hotels and restaurants are easy to find, and the food scene offers everything from traditional Kazakh dishes to Italian and Korean. Plan an evening to wander the river embankment and the central avenue, and eat well before the long northbound road. It is the best place on this route to fix a problem or find a part, so take advantage of it.
t.burabay@53.1,70.3:
Burabay is the place where Kazakhstan's flat steppe suddenly gives way to pine forest, granite outcrops and blue lakes. Rising from the plain in the north of the country, a cluster of low, rounded granite hills, weathered into odd shapes, surrounds a chain of lakes including Borovoe, Burabay and Shchuchye. Locals call it the Kazakh Switzerland, which is a stretch, but you understand the impulse after hundreds of kilometres of grassland.

The area is a national park, and a popular resort since Soviet times. Sanatoria, guesthouses and lakeside cafes line the shores, and in summer the beaches fill with families from Astana and beyond. Granite rocks have names and legends: Zhumbaktas, a sphinx-like block, and Okzhetpes, whose pointed top is said to be a place no arrow could reach, according to the story. Folklore and nature mix in the stories of khans and heroes who fought and hid here, and stone formations are said to be warriors or lovers turned to rock.

The ride from Astana is long and mostly straight, a couple of hundred kilometres across open steppe on a reasonable main road, with trucks, long vistas and a feeling that the sky is too big for the land. As you approach the hills, pine forest appears and the road becomes a little more varied, with gentle bends and shade. Mornings are cool and clear, and summer afternoons can bring thunderstorms. Watch for livestock, patches of rough tarmac and slow farm vehicles.

Burabay and the town of Shchuchinsk, a larger place about eighteen kilometres away, together provide good services. Fuel is available in Shchuchinsk, and in the resort area you will find hotels, restaurants and small shops. Fish from the lakes, along with kebabs and local dairy, feature on the menu. The best months are June to September; winter is deep, cold and silent. Spend an evening by the lake, walk a short trail onto the granite and watch the sun go down over the water.
t.karakoram highway point 3@34.9,72.9:
Besham is a loud, low-slung bazaar town where the highway meets the Indus, and for many riders it is the place where the Karakoram Highway stops being a road and becomes an adventure. The river here has just come out of a deep gorge, brown with silt and fast enough to hear above the engine. Mountains close in on both sides, the town is jammed into a narrow bench of land beside the water, and trucks park at every angle outside tea stalls.

The road from Mansehra, via Thakot and the bridge over the Indus, climbs and drops along steep slopes of loose rock. This is landslide country. In wet weather or after a cloudburst, sections can be blocked for hours or days, so check the news and ask a truck driver, because they know. The tarmac is generally good, but the edge is narrow, bends are blind, and the drop to the river is steep. Ride in daylight, keep right, and honk lightly before blind corners the way the locals do.

Besham is the junction for the road to Swat, which climbs west toward Mingora and the green valleys of the north. It is also a staging point for the Kohistan stretch that runs north. There is fuel here, and in the town you will find simple hotels, bakeries and rows of grills sending up smoke at dusk. Fill the tank, because fuel in the long Kohistan section can be unreliable and sometimes of questionable quality. Dal, flatbread and fried river fish are the usual fare, and tea is sweet and strong.

Behind the cheerful chaos, there is a landscape of real size. The Indus here cuts through the western end of the Himalaya, where geologists say the plates collided and the river has held its course while the mountains rose around it. The walls above are steep forests of pine and oak, and high summer brings terraced fields of maize. In winter, snow can reach the upper slopes, and the nights are cold.

Riders sometimes arrive late and stay overnight in Besham to break the long day from Islamabad. It is a sensible plan, since the road that follows is slow, the light fails early between the walls of the gorge, and the best part of the highway lies ahead.
t.near islamabad@33.7,73.0:
Islamabad is a planned city, and it looks it. Laid out in the early 1960s as a new capital for Pakistan to replace Karachi, it was designed by the Greek planner Constantinos Doxiadis on a grid of sectors, each with its own markets, schools and green spaces, and it sits at the foot of the Margalla Hills, the first wrinkles of the Himalayan foothills. Compared with the chaos of most South Asian cities, it is green, tidy and calm, with wide avenues and lots of trees. Next door, Rawalpindi, the old garrison town, is everything Islamabad is not: crowded, noisy, ancient and alive.

The city's great landmark is the Faisal Mosque, built in the 1980s with funding from Saudi Arabia and designed by the Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay. Its four minarets and tent-like prayer hall are inspired by a Bedouin tent rather than a traditional dome, and it is one of the largest mosques in the world, set against the green slopes of the Margalla Hills. The Pakistan Monument, shaped like the petals of a flower, stands on a hill on the other side of the city and has views over the whole capital, and the Daman-e-Koh viewpoint in the hills above is popular at sunset.

For riders heading north on the Karakoram Highway, Islamabad is the usual starting point, the place to sort out permits, insurance, money and supplies. The KKH proper begins at Hasan Abdal, north-west of the capital, and heads north through Abbottabad and Mansehra into the mountains. Traffic in and around Islamabad and Rawalpindi is heavy and chaotic, with buses, trucks, rickshaws and motorbikes all jostling for space, and the road out to the north can be slow until you get beyond Haripur.

Islamabad has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, workshops, hotels, restaurants, banks and good hospitals. It is the last place with this level of service until Gilgit, so sort out any mechanical issues here. The food is excellent: try chapli kebabs, karahi and fresh naan from a tandoor, and drink plenty of sweet milky chai. Check the security situation and any travel advisories before setting out, as conditions in some areas can change quickly. The best season for the KKH is from May to October, when the high passes are open.
